name: Magnesium malate
lead: Magnesium malate is the magnesium salt of malic acid, sold as an over-the-counter mineral supplement [1]. People in the fitness and recovery communities take it as a source of magnesium with the idea that adequate magnesium supports muscle function, post-workout soreness and sleep, which in turn supports more consistent training and, over time, a better physique.

Wikipedia notes that it is discussed as a more bioavailable form of magnesium than citrate or glycinate, citing a supplier web page [1]. Supplier and reference material also promote it for exercise recovery, muscle soreness and fibromyalgia pain [2]. In the T Nation lifting forum, members list it among their daily supplements, one describing magnesium as a muscle relaxer [7].

The European Food Safety Authority reviewed di-magnesium malate as a proposed novel food ingredient in 2018 [3]. Published bioavailability work comparing magnesium forms exists mainly in rodents [4][5], and one placebo-controlled human trial has examined a timed-release di-magnesium malate product [8].

paras: Magnesium malate consists of magnesium bound to malic acid, a dicarboxylic acid found naturally in fruits such as apples [1][2]. Reference text describes a white, hygroscopic powder, with a pentahydrate crystal form in which malate chelates the magnesium ion [2]. Products labelled di-magnesium malate contain two magnesium ions per malate and are the form evaluated by EFSA [3].

Malate is also an intermediate in the citric acid cycle, the cellular energy pathway. Supplement sellers draw on this when they describe the compound as supporting energy, although the link between ingested malate and measurable energy output in people is a marketing claim rather than a documented effect [2].

Magnesium malate has no direct cosmetic use. In bodybuilding and strength forums it appears in daily supplement lists alongside zinc, vitamin D and fish oil, with posters citing muscle relaxation, soreness and sleep as reasons [7][9][10]. The reasoning chain is recovery, then more consistent training, then muscle and physique.

It is used to supply magnesium where intake is low or absorption is reduced, such as malabsorption, chronic diarrhoea or diabetes [2]. Supplier materials and reference text also describe it for fibromyalgia pain and tenderness [2].

Magnesium is involved in muscle relaxation, and Wikipedia's biology entry describes magnesium ions as acting on cell membranes and blocking certain calcium channels, with inadequate intake often associated with muscle spasms.[12] ATP, the cell's main energy currency, has to be bound to a magnesium ion to be biologically active, and magnesium is also needed in the mitochondrial process that produces ATP.[12] These roles are the basis for the recovery and energy claims made for magnesium supplements generally, including the malate form.

US recommended dietary allowances for adults are listed as 400 to 420 mg per day for men and 310 to 320 mg per day for women, while the European Food Safety Authority's adequate intakes are 350 mg for men and 300 mg for women. Foods richest in magnesium include pumpkin and chia seeds, nuts, spinach, soybeans, whole grains and dark chocolate; refined foods are generally poor sources.[12] Deficiency from diet alone is described as uncommon and more often linked to chronic alcohol use, diuretics or prolonged intravenous feeding, with symptoms including spasms, fasciculations, irregular heartbeat and insomnia.[12]

Two 2019 studies from the same research group compared magnesium compounds in animals. In rats given a single dose, magnesium malate had the highest area under the curve among five compounds tested (sulfate, oxide, acetyl taurate, citrate and malate), and its levels stayed elevated for an extended period [4]. A second study gave mice three dose levels of citrate, malate, acetyl taurate and glycinate and examined tissue uptake and the effect of splitting high doses [5].

These are animal experiments. The Wikipedia entry attributes the claim of superior bioavailability to a supplier page [1], and EFSA concluded the data submitted did not show a difference between di-magnesium malate and the magnesium malate already authorised for supplements in the EU [3].

Reference summaries describe magnesium chloride, sulfate and citrate as absorbed at about 30 to 40 percent, oxide and hydroxide as absorbed erratically and less efficiently, and amino-acid chelates such as glycinate as better tolerated, with sustained-release products intended to limit diarrhea.[12] Another Wikipedia entry on magnesium supplements groups aspartate, chloride, lactate, citrate and glycinate as having similar absorption per unit of magnesium and roughly four times the bioavailability of oxide, and lists malate only among supplement forms without further detail.[13] This is the general context in which claims that malate is better absorbed are made; the comparative animal data for malate are described in the Bioavailability section above.

A 2018 pragmatic placebo-controlled trial in 91 adults at two US clinics tested a timed-release product containing 500 mg di-magnesium malate with vitamins B6, B12 and folate. Fifty-three people received the product. Serum magnesium was measured 4 and 8 hours after a first dose, red blood cell magnesium and a magnesium-status questionnaire were assessed at 30 days, and 24 participants continued to 90 days [8]. The product combined several ingredients, so results cannot be attributed to the malate salt alone.

Reference text describes small fibromyalgia trials reporting reduced pain and tenderness and athletes reporting less soreness, without trial details [2]. No study of the malate form on physique or muscle outcomes was found. A registered trial of a magnesium complex on body composition in 60 university students (NCT07906678) is listed as not yet recruiting [6].

EFSA's panel could not complete a safety assessment of di-magnesium malate as a novel ingredient because the applicant did not supply requested data; it stated that, if the compound dissociates, magnesium availability would appear similar to other authorised sources [3]. Magnesium malate itself is already listed as an authorised magnesium source for supplements in the EU [3].
Forum users commonly report taking amounts of 400 mg or more of elemental magnesium per day [7]; the supplement literature notes that higher oral magnesium intakes often cause bowel intolerance [8].

The US tolerable upper intake level for supplemental magnesium (not food magnesium) is 350 mg per day, and EFSA sets a lower limit of 250 mg per day.[12] Diarrhea is the most common side effect of excess oral magnesium, and poisoning is described as very rare in adults with normal kidney function because healthy kidneys excrete the excess. Infants should not receive magnesium supplements except under medical supervision.[12] Other effects listed for supplements include upset stomach, and hypermagnesemia, with nausea, low blood pressure, confusion and slowed heart rate, is described as possible only in special circumstances.[13]

On T Nation, magnesium malate shows up in members' supplement stacks and in advice threads. One poster described taking it for soreness and said magnesium is known as a muscle relaxer [7]. Another thread participant argued that supplements with only subjective findings are probably not worth buying, and named magnesium citrate among the researched examples [9]. Another member suggested getting magnesium malate with B6 and zinc as a lower-cost alternative to ZMA [11].

timeline.event: EFSA publishes its opinion on di-magnesium malate as a novel food ingredient [3]; a timed-release di-magnesium malate trial is published [8].
Two rodent studies compare bioavailability of magnesium compounds including malate [4][5].
A body-composition trial of a magnesium complex in university students is registered [6].

lore.intro: Magnesium malate is discussed in lifting forums as a recovery and sleep supplement, usually as one item in a larger stack [7][9][11].

claims.claim: Magnesium malate relaxes muscles and reduces soreness
claims.believers: A T Nation poster said they take it for soreness because magnesium is known as a muscle relaxer [7].
claims.experts: Reference text describes small trials in fibromyalgia and athlete soreness without trial details [2]. No controlled trial of the malate form on exercise-induced soreness was found.

claims.claim: Malate form is better absorbed than other magnesium salts
claims.believers: Supplement sellers and forum posters describe organic forms as better absorbed [1][11].
claims.experts: Rat data showed a higher exposure for malate than several forms [4], while EFSA found no demonstrated difference from already authorised magnesium malate [3].

claims.claim: It can replace ZMA as a cheaper magnesium source
claims.believers: A forum member suggested buying magnesium malate, B6 and zinc separately instead of ZMA [11].
claims.experts: No trial comparing these approaches was found.

card.summary: Magnesium bound to malic acid, pitched for energy, soreness and fibromyalgia; direct human evidence is thin.
card.note: Bioavailability superiority claims rest on supplier sources.

quick.overview:
Magnesium malate pairs magnesium with malic acid and is sold to correct deficiency and for muscle soreness and recovery.

Claims of better absorption come from a supplier source; EFSA has evaluated it as a food ingredient.
quick.mechanism: It supplies magnesium, which is involved in muscle and nerve function; malate is an intermediate in energy metabolism, which sellers cite for energy claims.
quick.risks: Human safety data specific to this form are limited in the sources; EFSA assessed its use in foods and supplements.

chain: Magnesium takes part in muscle contraction and relaxation and energy metabolism
Users report less soreness and easier recovery
More consistent training supports muscle and physique
angle.text: Lifters take magnesium malate as a magnesium source for muscle relaxation, soreness and sleep. The appearance benefit, as users describe it, comes from being able to train more consistently over time.
